cases.sentence: ___ знает только то, что успел узнать.
cases.translation: Reason knows only what it has managed to learn.
cases.explain: Рассудок is the subject of знает (knows), so it stands in the nominative.

cases.sentence: Мало того, тотчас же образится он из ___ в органный штифтик или вроде того.
cases.translation: What's more, he would immediately be transformed from a man into an organ pin or something like that.
cases.explain: The preposition из (out of) governs the genitive case, hence человека.

cases.sentence: Ну что за охота хотеть по ___?
cases.translation: What's the point of wanting anything according to a little chart?
cases.explain: The preposition по (according to) governs the dative case, hence табличке.
Реторту is the direct object of the transitive verb принять (accept), so it takes the accusative.

cases.sentence: Вы кричите мне, если только еще удостоите меня вашим ___, что ведь тут никто с меня воли не снимает.
cases.translation: You shout at me, if you'll still honor me with your shout, that no one is taking away my will here.
cases.explain: The verb удостоить (to honor someone with something) governs the instrumental case, hence криком.

cases.sentence: Одним словом, всё можно сказать о всемирной ___.
cases.translation: In a word, anything at all can be said about world history.
cases.explain: The preposition о (about) governs the prepositional case, hence истории.

reading.ru: Да ведь хотение-то в сущности, если хотите и нет, прерываете вы с хохотом. Наука даже о сю пор до того успеха разанатомировать человека, что уже теперь нам известно, что хотение и так, называемая свободной волей, есть не что иное, как...
reading.question: What has science supposedly discovered about human "wanting" (free will), according to the interrupting listeners?
options: That it has now dissected man to the point of explaining desire and free will scientifically
That free will does not exist and never did
That desire cannot be studied at all
That only animals have free will
reading.correct: That it has now dissected man to the point of explaining desire and free will scientifically
reading.explain: The interrupters claim that science has now dissected man to such an extent that it already knows what desire and so-called free will really are.

reading.ru: Ну что за охота хотеть по табличке? Мало того, тотчас же образится он из человека в органный штифтик или вроде того, потому что же такое человек без желаний, без воли и без хотений, как не штифтик в органном вале?
reading.question: What does the narrator sarcastically say man would turn into if his desires could be calculated like a chart?
options: An organ pin or something similar
reading.correct: An organ pin or something similar
reading.explain: He says man would immediately be transformed from a man into an organ pin or something of that sort, since what is man without desires and will?

reading.ru: то тогда, разумеется, не будет так называемых желаний.
reading.question: What does the narrator predict would happen to "so-called desires" once everything is calculated and explained?
options: There would be no such thing as desires anymore
Desires would become stronger than ever
reading.correct: There would be no such thing as desires anymore
reading.explain: He concludes that once everything is explained and calculated, there will no longer be so-called desires at all.

reading.ru: Ведь я тогда вперед. Всю мою жизнь на 30 лет рассчитать могу.
reading.question: What does the narrator imagine being able to do if a scientist could calculate his life?
options: Calculate his entire life thirty years in advance
Change his own fate at will
reading.correct: Calculate his entire life thirty years in advance
reading.explain: He imagines that if he were a scholar, he could calculate his whole life thirty years ahead.

reading.ru: Надо принять реторту.
reading.question: What does the narrator say must be accepted, even if reluctantly?
options: The retort (a symbol of scientific determinism)
reading.correct: The retort (a symbol of scientific determinism)
reading.explain: He concludes flatly, "One must accept the retort," referring to the scientific, deterministic view of man.

reading.ru: Тут 40 лет подполье.
reading.question: How long does the narrator say he has spent in the "underground"?
reading.correct: Forty years
reading.explain: He states plainly, "Forty years of underground here," referring to his long life of underground brooding.

reading.ru: А хотение есть проявление всей жизни, то есть всей человеческой жизни, и с рассудком, и со всеми подчесываниями.
reading.question: What does the narrator claim "wanting" (desire/will) is a manifestation of?
options: The whole of life, including reason and everything else
Pure irrationality with no connection to reason
A disease that should be cured
reading.correct: The whole of life, including reason and everything else
reading.explain: He argues that desire is a manifestation of the whole of life — all of human life, together with reason and everything else in it.

reading.ru: Что знает рассудок? Рассудок знает только то, что успел узнать.
reading.question: What limitation does the narrator identify in what "reason" (рассудок) can know?
options: Reason knows only what it has managed to learn, and may never learn other things
reading.correct: Reason knows only what it has managed to learn, and may never learn other things
reading.explain: He asks what reason knows, answering that reason knows only what it has managed to learn, and other things it perhaps never will.

reading.ru: И хоть врет, да живет.
reading.question: What paradox does the narrator state about human nature lying but still living?
options: "It cannot lie because it does not live"
reading.correct: "Though it lies, it still lives"
reading.explain: He states the paradox plainly: "And though it lies, it still lives" (И хоть врет, да живет).

reading.ru: Ведь это глупейшее, ведь это свой каприз.
reading.question: How does the narrator describe the one exception where a man may consciously wish himself something harmful?
options: As the stupidest thing, but as his own caprice
As a sign of true wisdom
As something forbidden by reason alone
reading.correct: As the stupidest thing, but as his own caprice
reading.explain: He admits it is the stupidest thing, but insists it is his own caprice — his right to want it.

reading.ru: Действительно, ведь никак нельзя этого сказать про него, хоть бы по тому одному, что если уж он будет глуп, так ведь кто же тогда будет умен? Но если и не глуп, то все-таки чудовищно неблагодарен.
reading.question: What does the narrator concede and then immediately add about man's intelligence and gratitude?
options: Man cannot really be called stupid, but he is monstrously ungrateful
Man is both stupid and ungrateful in equal measure
Man is neither stupid nor ungrateful
Man is stupid but always grateful
reading.correct: Man cannot really be called stupid, but he is monstrously ungrateful
reading.explain: He concedes one cannot really call man stupid, but insists that even so, man is monstrously ungrateful.

reading.ru: Я даже думаю, что самое лучшее определение человека – это существо на двух ногах неблагодарное.
reading.question: What does the narrator propose as the best possible definition of man?
options: A two-legged creature that is ungrateful
A being made in the image of God
A creature ruled entirely by instinct
reading.correct: A two-legged creature that is ungrateful
reading.explain: He proposes that the best definition of man is "a two-legged creature that is ungrateful."

reading.ru: Главнейший недостаток его – это постоянное неблагонравие. Постоянное, начиная от всемирного потопа до Шлезвиг-Гольштейнского периода судеб человеческих.
reading.question: What does the narrator call man's chief flaw, tracing it from the Flood to the Schleswig-Holstein affair?
reading.correct: Constant unseemliness/impropriety (неблагонравие)
reading.explain: He names man's chief flaw as constant impropriety, tracing it all the way from the universal Flood to the Schleswig-Holstein period.

reading.ru: Пожалуй, хоть и величественно, уж один колосс Сарадовский, например, чего стоит.
reading.question: What example does the narrator sarcastically raise when asked what is "majestic" in human history?
options: The Colossus of Rhodes (referenced here as "the Saradov colossus")
reading.correct: The Colossus of Rhodes (referenced here as "the Saradov colossus")
reading.explain: He sarcastically cites a great colossus as an example of something one might call majestic in human history.

reading.ru: Дерутся, да дерутся. И теперь дерутся, и прежде дрались, и после дрались.
reading.question: What repetitive human activity throughout history does the narrator highlight with the phrase "they fight, and they fight"?
reading.correct: Fighting/warfare, now, before, and after
reading.explain: He notes that people fight and fight — they fought before, they fight now, and they will fight after, calling it monotonous.

reading.ru: Постоянно ведь являются в жизни такие благонравные и благоразумные люди, такие мудрецы и любители рода человеческого. которые именно задаются себе целью всю жизнь вести себя как можно благонравнее и благоразумнее, так сказать, светить собой ближним, собственно, для того, чтобы доказать им, что действительно можно на свете прожить и благонравно, и благоразумно, и что...
reading.question: What kind of people does the narrator say are constantly appearing in life, setting themselves the goal of living virtuously?
options: Well-behaved and prudent people, sages and lovers of mankind
reading.correct: Well-behaved and prudent people, sages and lovers of mankind
reading.explain: He notes that well-behaved, prudent people, sages and lovers of humanity, constantly appear who set themselves the goal of living as virtuously as possible.

reading.ru: И что ж, известно, многие из этих любителей рано или поздно, или под конец жизни, изменяли себе, произведя какой-нибудь анекдот, иногда даже из самых неприличнейших.
reading.question: What eventually happens to many of these virtuous "lovers of mankind," according to the narrator?
options: Sooner or later, often near the end of their lives, they betray themselves with some scandalous incident
They are always remembered fondly forever
They convert everyone else to virtue
reading.correct: Sooner or later, often near the end of their lives, they betray themselves with some scandalous incident
reading.explain: He observes that many of these lovers of mankind, sooner or later, often at the end of life, betrayed themselves by producing some indecent anecdote.

reading.ru: И тут из одной неблагодарности, из одного пасквиля мерзость сделает, рискнет даже пряниками и нарочно пожелает самого пагубного вздора, самой неэкономической бессмыслицы, единственно для того, чтобы ко всему этому положительному благоразумию примешать свой пагубный фантастический элемент, именно свои фантастические мечты, свою пошлейшую грубость.
reading.question: What would man do out of sheer ingratitude, even if given every comfort and blessing?
options: Commit some vile act, risking even his gingerbread, out of pure ingratitude
Become perfectly content and stop complaining
Give away all his comforts to others
reading.correct: Commit some vile act, risking even his gingerbread, out of pure ingratitude
reading.explain: He argues that out of sheer ingratitude, man would commit some vileness, risking even his gingerbread treats, just to prove he is not a piano key.

reading.ru: Да ведь мало того, даже в том случае, если он действительно бы оказался фортепианной клавишей, если бы это доказать ему даже естественными науками и математически, так и тут не образумится, а нарочно, напротив, что-нибудь сделать, единственно и с одной неблагодарностью, собственно, чтобы настоять на своем.
reading.question: What does the narrator say man would do even if it were proven, mathematically, that he really is a piano key?
options: He would still not come to his senses, and would deliberately do something out of sheer ingratitude
He would happily accept the fact and become perfectly obedient
He would thank the scientists who proved it
reading.correct: He would still not come to his senses, and would deliberately do something out of sheer ingratitude
reading.explain: He insists that even if man were proven mathematically to be a piano key, he still would not come to his senses, but would act out of pure ingratitude to insist on his own way.

reading.ru: Проклятие пустят по свету, а так как проклинать может только один человек, это уже его привилегия, главнейшим образом отличающая его от других животных. Так ведь он, пожалуй, одним проклятием достигнет своего, то есть действительно убедится, что он человек, а не фортепианная клавиша.
reading.question: What privilege does the narrator say belongs only to man, distinguishing him from other animals?
options: The ability to curse/utter a curse (проклятие)
reading.correct: The ability to curse/utter a curse (проклятие)
reading.explain: He notes that only man can curse, and this is his privilege, chiefly distinguishing him from other animals — and by this curse alone he may prove that he is a man and not a piano key.

reading.ru: Так человек нарочно сумасшедшим на этот случай сделается, чтобы... не иметь рассудка и настоять на своем я верю в это я отвечаю за это потому что ведь все дело человеческое кажется и действительно в том только и состоит чтобы человек поминутно доказывала себе что он человека не штифтик хоть своими боками да доказывал хоть троглодитством да доказывал а после этого как не согрешить не похвалить что этого еще нет, и что хотение покамест еще черт знает от чего зависит.
reading.question: What does the narrator say man would deliberately do, even to prove he lacks reason and to have his own way?
options: Deliberately go mad, for that very purpose
Deliberately give away all his possessions
reading.correct: Deliberately go mad, for that very purpose
reading.explain: He claims man would deliberately make himself insane for this very occasion, in order not to have reason and to insist on his own way.

reading.ru: Такая ли своя воля бывает?
reading.question: What rhetorical question does the narrator ask about "one's own will" once everything reduces to arithmetic (twice two is four)?
options: Whether that can really be called one's own will at all
Whether will exists only in mathematics
Whether will is stronger than reason
reading.correct: Whether that can really be called one's own will at all
reading.explain: He asks mockingly, "Is that really one's own will?" once everything comes down to twice two is four, whether you will it or not.
